personality_voice.book_baseline: Hagrid in the books is warm, loyal, physically imposing, and instinctively protective. His voice is immediately distinctive: phonetic dialect ('yeh', 'ter', 'bin', ''em'), short emphatic sentences, emotional outbursts, and a pattern of blurting things out before catching himself. He is proud of magical creatures, easily embarrassed when caught in minor rule-bending (the Engorgement Charm on pumpkins, the umbrella wand), and deeply devoted to those he loves. He is also quick to anger in defense of his friends — bursting into Dumbledore's office waving a dead rooster to defend Harry, leaping to his feet at Fudge's arrival, shouting at Lucius Malfoy. He has a comic side (the treacle fudge cementing Harry's jaws, teasing Harry about Ginny), but it never undercuts his emotional sincerity. He is not especially self-aware and tends to miss social subtleties, but his moral compass is unerring.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves all of Hagrid's core vocal and behavioral markers. His dialect is intact throughout: 'Yer a mess! Skulkin' round Knockturn Alley', 'Better out than in', 'Yeh can take Dumbledore! Take him away an' the Muggle-borns won' stand a chance!' His warmth and protectiveness are present in the Knockturn Alley rescue, the slug scene in his hut, the Azkaban confrontation. The embarrassed self-correction when Harry asks what he was doing in Knockturn Alley, the defensive outrage when Fudge arrives, the tearful return at the end — all consistent with the book character. His comic timing is preserved (the crossbow, the 'Rogue Bludger' commentary from the stands). The Quidditch commentary adds a small book-consistent beat. The cut 'Harry runs into Hagrid' scene removes one corridor encounter with the dead rooster, but the same rooster prop and purpose appear in the Dumbledore's office scene, so the personality texture is not lost there.
personality_voice.difference: Minor. The film loses the extended hut scene texture — the treacle fudge moment, the gentle teasing about Ginny and Harry, the jokes about Lockhart — which build a richer portrait of Hagrid's domestic warmth and humor. The book also shows Hagrid's knowing wink about Ginny's crush, a small but characteristic moment of sly social observation that is absent in the film. The film Hagrid is slightly more reactive and less verbally playful in the hut scene, which is compressed. His pride in his pumpkins and the implied wand-in-umbrella detail are both absent.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — voice, dialect, warmth, protectiveness, emotional directness, comic embarrassment — is fully preserved. The losses are in textural richness rather than in defining traits. The film Hagrid is recognizably and faithfully the book Hagrid in personality and voice. A small deduction is appropriate for the compression of the hut scene warmth and humor, and the absence of the pumpkin-pride / umbrella-wand moment, which adds a layer of lovable rule-bending complexity.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Hagrid serves several distinct narrative functions in CoS: (1) a safe harbor and emotional anchor for Harry and his friends — his cabin is where they go when distressed; (2) an information provider — he explains Mudblood, defends Hermione, explains the Dark Arts job jinx, and crucially provides the 'follow the spiders' clue that drives the forest plot; (3) a physical intervener — he separates the Weasley-Malfoy brawl in Flourish and Blotts; (4) a moral compass — his defense of Harry to Dumbledore and his outrage at Fudge and Lucius Malfoy demonstrate his values in action; (5) a plot object — his arrest and absence create stakes and motivate Harry and Ron's forest visit; (6) a past protagonist — the diary vision reveals his teenage role in the Chamber mystery. He initiates several scenes: he finds Harry in Knockturn Alley, he bursts into Dumbledore's office unprompted, he gives the 'follow the spiders' clue. His agency in the bookshop brawl is physical and decisive.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: All six functions are preserved in the film, though with varying fidelity. The Knockturn Alley rescue is intact. The Flourish and Blotts intervention is adapted: in the book Hagrid physically separates the fighting men, while in the film the fight does not escalate to the same physical level — Mr. Weasley moves to hit Malfoy and Hagrid's hand on his shoulder stops it. The 'follow the spiders' clue is preserved and is in fact given more dramatic weight, delivered as a carefully coded farewell message in front of Fudge. Hagrid's defense of Harry to Dumbledore (the rooster scene) is present. His emotional anchor function in the hut scene is compressed but present. His return at the end is given a celebratory beat. The diary vision of Young Hagrid is faithful.
narrative_role_agency.difference: In the bookshop scene, the book has Hagrid physically pulling the two men apart after an actual brawl; in the film he merely prevents the fight from starting. This is a small but real reduction in agency — in the books he is the one who physically ends the confrontation, while in the film he restrains rather than separates. The extended hut visit in the books has Hagrid providing more narrative information (the jinxed DADA position, Lockhart critique, pumpkin growing) that is cut. The cut 'Harry runs into Hagrid' corridor scene removes a moment of Hagrid noticing Harry's distress and asking after him — a small check-in beat that shows his attentiveness. This beat is not replaced in the film.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The main narrative functions are preserved. The 'follow the spiders' clue — Hagrid's most plot-critical contribution — is present and well-executed. The bookshop agency reduction is real but modest. The lost corridor scene removes a small attentiveness beat but does not substantially alter his narrative function. A moderate deduction is warranted for the physical agency reduction in the bookshop and the compression of information-giving in the hut.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Hagrid's motivations in CoS are consistent and clear: loyalty to Harry and his friends, fierce protectiveness of those he loves (human and creature), deep attachment to Hogwarts as his home and identity, and an instinctive, sometimes naive love of dangerous creatures. His internal conflict is not dramatized explicitly but is embedded in his behavior: he knows he bends rules (the Engorgement Charm, the wand concealed in his umbrella) and is embarrassed when caught; he loves Aragog despite knowing the spider cannot fully restrain its nature; he is terrified of Azkaban and of losing his place at Hogwarts, which is everything to him. The scene where he is trembling as Fudge arrives, repeating 'I never' to Dumbledore, shows the fear beneath the bluster. His motivation to protect Harry is so strong that he bursts into Dumbledore's office with a dead rooster to defend him before anyone can accuse.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core motivations: loyalty to Harry, protectiveness, love of Hogwarts. The trembling and 'I never' before Dumbledore and Fudge are present. The 'follow the spiders' moment is motivated by the same protective instinct — giving Harry a tool to clear both their names. The Young Hagrid scene in the diary vision shows the same creature-loyalty motivation. The fear of Azkaban is explicit ('Not Azkaban prison'). However, the internal complexity around his rule-bending — the Engorgement Charm on the pumpkins, the umbrella wand — is absent, removing the layer of Hagrid as a character who bends rules out of innocent enthusiasm and is slightly ashamed of it when caught. This is a recurring book pattern that adds texture to his motivation structure.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film loses the embedded rule-bending motivation pattern (Engorgement Charm, umbrella wand) and the mild self-consciousness it generates. The DADA job jinx explanation, which in the books shows Hagrid's insider knowledge and his loyalty to Hogwarts by contextualizing Lockhart's presence, is absent. These are motivational textures, not core motivations. The core — loyalty, protectiveness, love of Hogwarts — is intact.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Core motivations are present. The loss of the rule-bending texture simplifies his character somewhat but does not change who he fundamentally is or why he acts. A moderate deduction is appropriate for the flattening of his self-aware rule-bending motivation pattern, which in the books is a recurring, distinctive trait.

character_arc.book_baseline: Hagrid's arc in CoS is not a transformative personal arc but a structural one: he begins as a trusted, present anchor figure; is then removed from the story (arrested, taken to Azkaban) in a way that creates both plot stakes and emotional absence; and is restored at the end, his innocence vindicated. The arc also has a backstory dimension — the diary vision reveals the teenage Hagrid who was framed by Riddle, adding a layer of historical injustice to his character. The emotional journey is: trusted friend → suspected and imprisoned → exonerated and welcomed back. His return is a moral restoration, not merely a plot convenience. The book emphasizes the wrongness of his arrest by showing the castle's wrongness without him ('no Hagrid visible from the castle windows... the scene didn't look right to Harry').
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film follows the same structural arc. Hagrid is present, arrested, absent, and returned. His return scene is given significant emotional weight — the hall going silent, his embarrassed speech, Harry's 'There's no Hogwarts without you, Hagrid', the standing ovation. The diary vision of Young Hagrid is faithful and provides the same backstory dimension. The film makes the 'follow the spiders' moment his key active contribution before arrest, which is structurally sound.
character_arc.difference: The film does not include the narrative description of the castle feeling wrong without Hagrid, which in the book explicitly articulates his symbolic importance to Hogwarts. This is a minor loss of arc emphasis rather than a structural omission. The arc steps — trusted presence, arrest, absence, restoration — are all present.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but faithful. All major steps are present. The loss of the 'castle feels wrong without him' narration is a minor emotional emphasis loss, not a structural arc change. The restoration scene is well-executed. A small deduction for the missing emotional articulation of the absence phase.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Hagrid's key relationships in CoS are: (1) Harry — a bond of affection, care, and mutual protectiveness; Hagrid is one of Harry's few genuine adult allies; (2) Dumbledore — deep loyalty and trust, Hagrid's deference to Dumbledore is absolute, and Dumbledore's reciprocal confidence in Hagrid ('Hagrid has my full confidence') is a significant plot beat; (3) the Weasleys — warm familiarity, particularly with Ron; (4) Aragog — a relationship that reveals Hagrid's complex love of creatures and the consequences of his naivety; (5) Lucius Malfoy — open contempt and hostility, Hagrid representing the opposite of Malfoy's values.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Hagrid bond is present in the Knockturn Alley scene, the hut visit, and most powerfully in the end scene where Harry's 'There's no Hogwarts without you, Hagrid' is a direct and warm expression of the relationship. The Dumbledore-Hagrid loyalty is intact in both the office scene and the Azkaban confrontation. The Aragog relationship is present and carries its book dynamic — Hagrid's protective love, the complexity that even Aragog cannot fully protect his friends. The Malfoy hostility is present in both the bookshop and the hut scene. The Weasley warmth is present but reduced.
key_relationships.difference: The extended hut scene in the books builds the Hagrid-Harry-Ron-Hermione relational warmth more fully through shared tea, jokes, and the Ginny teasing. The film compresses this. The Hagrid-Hermione dynamic (Hagrid calling her 'our Hermione' with pride, making her blush) is present in the film's hut scene but in a slightly reduced form. The Ginny teasing moment — which links Hagrid's warmth and comic side — is absent in the film.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: All key relationships are present and their core dynamics are preserved. The losses are in warmth and texture rather than in relational structure or emotional function. A small deduction for the compression of the hut relational texture and the absent Ginny-teasing beat.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Hagrid's complexity in CoS comes from several layered sources: (1) his rule-bending with the Engorgement Charm and concealed wand — he is not fully law-abiding, just innocently transgressive; (2) his instinct for dangerous creatures that Ron explicitly names as a character flaw ('That's exactly Hagrid's problem! He always thinks monsters aren't as bad as they're made out'); (3) his critical opinion of Lockhart, which is unusual for him since he rarely criticizes colleagues, and which is delivered with dry wit ('If one word of it was true, I'll eat my kettle') and sly humor (telling Lockhart he'd never read his books); (4) his domestic warmth — the treacle fudge, the overflowing copper basin, the cheerful 'better out than in'; (5) the historical injustice of his framing — Riddle's contemptuous description of 'big, blundering Hagrid' and the clear unfairness of the word of a star pupil against a disadvantaged boy; (6) his coded farewell ('follow the spiders') under observation, showing situational intelligence.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves: the creature-loyalty flaw (Ron's 'follow the spiders' complaint, 'if he ever gets out of Azkaban I'll kill Hagrid'), the Lockhart criticism (the hut scene includes Hagrid's skepticism), the historical injustice (the diary vision, Tom Riddle's framing), and the coded farewell. What is lost: the Engorgement Charm / umbrella wand texture, the Lockhart dry wit ('I'll eat my kettle', the 'never read his books' exit line — the latter IS present in the film: 'An' I told him I'd never read one o' his books an' he decided ter go'), the treacle fudge comedy, the Ginny-teasing. The film Lockhart scepticism is somewhat preserved. The umbrella wand is entirely absent, removing a recurring complexity marker.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The key losses are: the umbrella wand (a recurring CoS book detail that adds a dimension of sympathetic rule-breaking and backstory), the pumpkin Engorgement Charm, the treacle fudge comedy sequence, and the Ginny teasing. These collectively represent a reduction in Hagrid's domestic-warmth-and-minor-transgression texture. The creature-flaw and historical-injustice dimensions are well-preserved.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The film preserves the most important complexity markers — the creature flaw, the framing injustice, the coded intelligence of 'follow the spiders', the Lockhart skepticism. The losses are real but concentrated in domestic and comic texture rather than in the character's defining contradictions or moral complexity. A moderate deduction is appropriate: the character is not flattened into one trait, but a notable layer of nuance (the rule-bending, the domestic comedy) is missing.

lost_or_transferred_material: Engorgement Charm on pumpkins scene — Hagrid's rule-bending with the concealed umbrella wand, showing sympathetic transgression and embarrassment when caught
Treacle fudge cementing Harry's jaws shut — a comic domestic moment revealing Hagrid's warmth and inadvertent physicality
Hagrid teasing Harry about Ginny's crush — a moment of sly social observation and warm humor
Hagrid's explanation of the DADA job jinx — showing insider Hogwarts knowledge and loyalty

Hagrid telling Lockhart 'I'll eat my kettle' if one word of his books is true — dry skeptical wit (the 'never read his books' line is partially preserved in the film but the full exchange is compressed)
Book narration of the castle feeling wrong without Hagrid during his absence — explicit articulation of his symbolic importance to Hogwarts

The bookshop brawl: in the book Hagrid physically separates the fighting men after actual blows are exchanged; in the film he merely restrains Mr. Weasley before the fight escalates — a reduction in physical agency
The corridor encounter where Hagrid notices Harry looking distressed and checks on him (cut scene per exclusion note — counts as lost material)
Riddle's full contemptuous monologue about 'big, blundering Hagrid' in the books is slightly more extended than in the film, with more detail about Hagrid's rule-breaking reputation at school
score_caps_applied: Cap 1 considered (above 85 if films remove major complexity): total is below 85, cap not binding but complexity losses noted

Cap 3 considered (above 75 if core book function transferred): the bookshop physical intervention is reduced but not fully transferred; cap at 75 not applied as the reduction is partial rather than a full transfer of agency to another character
key_observations: Hagrid is one of the more faithfully adapted characters in Chamber of Secrets. His voice, dialect, warmth, protectiveness, and moral directness are all preserved with high fidelity. The film successfully captures his most important narrative functions: the Knockturn Alley rescue, the slug scene, the Azkaban confrontation, the 'follow the spiders' clue, and the vindicated return. The primary losses are concentrated in domestic texture and minor rule-bending complexity — the pumpkin Engorgement Charm, the umbrella wand, the treacle fudge comedy, and the Ginny teasing — which together reduce the richness of his character without changing its essential shape. A secondary loss is his reduced physical agency in the bookshop scene, where in the book he physically separates two men who have already come to blows, while in the film he prevents the fight before it begins. The film Hagrid is recognizably and substantially the book Hagrid; the score of 79 reflects genuine fidelity in core dimensions with meaningful but not devastating losses in complexity and nuance.
